lesson.text: Quick memory: in a moving picture, what makes a good pivot? (A paper fastener.) Today: choosing the right tool, and using it safely, always with a grown-up.
Choose the right tool: scissors cut paper, card and thread; a junior hacksaw cuts wood; a hole punch makes neat holes; a ruler and pencil measure and mark; sandpaper smooths rough edges.
Hold it still: before sawing, hold the wood in a bench hook or a clamp, so your hands stay away from the blade. Saw slowly, with long, gentle strokes.
Protect yourself: wear goggles when sawing or drilling, an apron for glue and paint, and tie back long hair.
Carry scissors closed, with the points down. To pass them, hold the closed blades and offer the handles.
Workshop rules: one person, one tool, one job. Never run with tools. Put each tool back in its place, and tell a grown-up about anything broken, or any cut.
Joining: glue is strong but needs time to dry, and tape can hold the parts while it does. Card triangles glued on the corners make a wooden frame stronger.
Try it in the world: build a workshop with a tool wall, where every tool has its own place, and a sign with your three workshop rules.

exercises.prompt: Match each tool to its job.
exercises.hint: Think of what each tool is for.
exercises.explain: Scissors cut paper and card, a junior hacksaw cuts wood, sandpaper smooths edges, a ruler measures.

exercises.hint: What keeps the points away from people?
exercises.explain: Closed, with the points down, walking.

exercises.prompt: You should wear goggles when sawing or drilling.
exercises.hint: What could fly into your eyes?
exercises.explain: True: goggles stop dust and chips getting into your eyes.

exercises.prompt: Which tool cuts a strip of wood?
exercises.hint: It has a blade with teeth.
exercises.explain: A junior hacksaw, with the wood held still in a bench hook.

exercises.prompt: What holds wood still while you saw it?
exercises.hint: Your hands must stay away from the blade.
choices: a bench hook or a clamp
exercises.explain: A bench hook or a clamp holds the wood, so your hands stay safe.

exercises.prompt: Is it safe or not safe in the workshop?
items: leave a spill on the floor
test a blade on your finger
exercises.hint: Would it keep everyone free from harm?
exercises.explain: Safe: tie hair back, put tools back, goggles. Not safe: running with scissors, spills, testing blades on fingers.

exercises.prompt: Put cutting a strip of wood in order.
exercises.hint: Measure and mark before you cut.
items: measure the length with a ruler
hold the wood in a bench hook
exercises.explain: Measure, mark, hold it in a bench hook, saw on the line, then sand the end smooth.

exercises.prompt: It is fine to pass scissors with the blades pointing at your friend.
exercises.explain: False: hold the closed blades and offer the handles.

exercises.prompt: Bram's sawn wood has rough, splintery ends. Which tool helps?
exercises.hint: Which tool makes rough edges smooth?

exercises.prompt: Why keep both hands away from the saw blade?
choices: so it cannot cut you if it slips
exercises.explain: If the saw slips, it cannot cut a hand that is not near it.

exercises.prompt: Mimi is gluing two pieces of card and the glue is still wet. What helps?
choices: tape to hold them while it dries
exercises.explain: Tape holds the pieces in place while the glue dries.

exercises.prompt: Zara's wooden frame is wobbly at the corners. What can she add?
exercises.hint: Remember which shape makes frames strong.
choices: card triangles glued on the corners
exercises.explain: Card triangles on each corner stop the joints moving, so the frame is stronger.

exercises.prompt: 'One person, one tool, one job' helps keep a workshop safe.
exercises.hint: What could go wrong with two on one tool?
exercises.explain: True: one person using one tool for one job at a time means no one gets in the way of a blade.

exercises.prompt: What should you do if a tool is broken?
exercises.hint: A broken tool can hurt someone.
exercises.explain: Stop using it and tell a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: Sort the safety steps by when you need them.
exercises.hint: Which ones stop chips and blades, which stop mess, and which are rules for every job?
exercises.explain: Sawing or drilling: goggles and a bench hook. Gluing and painting: an apron. Every job: tie back long hair and put tools back in their place.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to the safe fix.
items: the wood wobbles as you saw
matches: hold it in a bench hook
exercises.hint: Think of the workshop rules on cards 2 to 5.
exercises.explain: Wobbly wood: hold it in a bench hook. Long hair: tie it back. Passing scissors: hold the closed blades and offer the handles. A cut: tell a grown-up.
